questions.question: What is the main problem that consistent hashing solves?
options: Reducing database query latency
Minimizing data movement when nodes are added or removed
Encrypting data in transit between servers
Compressing data for efficient storage
questions.explanation: When using simple modular hashing (key % N), adding or removing a server changes N, causing almost ALL keys to remap. Consistent hashing ensures only ~K/N keys need to move when a node joins or leaves the cluster.

questions.question: In a consistent hashing ring, how are keys assigned to nodes?
options: Keys are randomly distributed across all available nodes
Each key is assigned to the nearest node clockwise on the ring
Keys are assigned based on alphabetical order of node names
Each key is replicated to every node on the ring
questions.explanation: In a consistent hashing ring, both keys and nodes are mapped to positions on the ring using a hash function. Each key is then assigned to the first node encountered when walking clockwise from the key's position on the ring.

questions.question: When a single server is removed from a consistent hashing ring with N servers, approximately what fraction of keys need to be remapped?
options: All keys must be remapped
Approximately 1/N of the keys
Approximately 50% of the keys
No keys need to be remapped
questions.explanation: When one server is removed, only the keys that were assigned to that server need to move -- roughly 1/N of all keys. Those keys simply migrate to the next node clockwise on the ring, leaving all other assignments untouched.

questions.question: What happens with simple modulo hashing (key % N) when a server is added to a cluster of N servers?
options: Only 1/N of the keys need to be remapped
No keys need to be remapped
Almost all keys need to be remapped to different servers
Exactly half the keys need to be remapped
questions.explanation: With modulo hashing, changing N to N+1 alters the result of key % N for nearly every key. This causes a rehashing cascade where the vast majority of keys must be moved to different servers, creating a massive data migration event.

questions.question: What are virtual nodes (vnodes) in consistent hashing, and why are they used?
options: Backup nodes that activate only when a primary node fails
Multiple hash positions per physical node to improve load balance
Virtual machines that run inside physical servers
Temporary nodes used during cluster scaling operations
questions.explanation: Virtual nodes map each physical server to multiple positions on the hash ring. This improves load distribution because a server with more capacity can own more vnodes, and the many ring positions create a more uniform spread of key ownership.

questions.question: Which real-world distributed systems use consistent hashing as a core mechanism?
options: MySQL and PostgreSQL for query optimization
Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, and Memcached
Linux kernel and Windows OS for memory management
HTTP and TCP protocols for packet routing
questions.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB and Apache Cassandra both use consistent hashing to partition data across nodes in their distributed clusters. Memcached clients also use it to distribute cache keys. These systems rely on consistent hashing to minimize disruption during scaling.

questions.question: When a new server is added to a consistent hashing ring, which existing server(s) give up keys to the new node?
options: All servers redistribute an equal share of their keys
Only the server that is the new node's clockwise successor on the ring
The two servers closest to the new node
A random subset of servers selected by the load balancer
questions.explanation: The new node takes a position on the ring and assumes ownership of keys that now fall in its range. These keys all previously belonged to the new node's immediate clockwise successor, so only that one server needs to transfer data.

questions.question: Without virtual nodes, consistent hashing can produce uneven load. If 3 nodes are placed on a ring with hash space 0-359, and they hash to positions 10, 20, and 350, what fraction of keys does the node at position 350 own?
options: Approximately 1/3 of the keys
Approximately 10/360 of the keys
Approximately 330/360 of the keys
Approximately 170/360 of the keys
questions.explanation: The node at position 350 owns all keys from position 21 to 350, which spans 330 units out of 360. This means it owns roughly 91.7% of all keys. This severe imbalance is exactly why virtual nodes are necessary for practical deployments.

questions.question: What is 'consistent hashing with bounded loads' and what problem does it address?
options: A variant that limits the hash ring to a fixed size to reduce memory usage
A technique that caps maximum load per node to within a factor of the average, preventing hotspots
A method that bounds the number of servers in the cluster for predictable performance
An encryption layer that limits data exposure per node for security compliance
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing with bounded loads (proposed by Mirrokni et al.) sets a capacity threshold per node, typically (1 + epsilon) times the average load. When a node is full, keys overflow to the next node on the ring, preventing any single node from becoming a hotspot.

questions.question: In a system using consistent hashing with 150 virtual nodes per server, you need to add 2 new physical servers to a 10-server cluster. Approximately how many key migrations will occur if the cluster holds 1 million keys?
options: Approximately 1,000,000 keys (all keys)
Approximately 500,000 keys
Approximately 166,667 keys
Approximately 20,000 keys
questions.explanation: Adding 2 servers to a 10-server cluster means the new servers will each claim ~1/12 of the ring space, together absorbing ~2/12 or ~1/6 of total keys. So approximately 1,000,000 / 6 = 166,667 keys need to migrate. Virtual nodes help ensure this migration is spread evenly across existing servers.
